newsitem.title: USA: California shows tough new anti-smoking ads.
newsitem.headline: California shows tough new anti-smoking ads.

text.p: California previewed tough new anti-smoking advertisements on Thursday, including a shocking television spot showing a cancer sufferer smoking a cigarette through a hole in her neck.

"This advertising is some of the most aggressive, hard-hitting material that California's tobacco education media campaign has ever produced," said Sandra Smoley, secretary of California's Health and Welfare Agency.

The ads were paid for by a 25-cent tax on cigarettes approved by California voters in 1988. Part of the proceeds are used to fund tobacco education programs, including anti-tobacco advertising campaigns that began in 1989.

The latest package of ads includes six television commercials, six radio spots and four outdoor print ads, all created by a Los Angeles advertising agency. The state will spend $13 million on buying space for the ads, which cost another $2 million to produce. The ads will be released statewide starting next Monday.
California Health Director Kim Belshe said the state's aim was to give smokers and non-smokers powerful reasons "to either quit or never start using tobacco to begin with."
The ads underscore the dangers of second-hand smoke and the addictive nature of nicotine while other spots were aimed at countering smoking among teen-agers and young adults, she said.

The hardest-hitting ad features a 46-year-old woman who began smoking when she was 13 and lost her larynx to throat cancer in 1992. The woman, called Debi, says: "They say nicotine isn't addictive." She picks up a cigarette from an ashtray and draws on it through a hole in her throat before adding: "How can they say that?"
A second television ad shows sinister cowboys herding frightened children into a pen in what Belshe says is a "metaphor for the marketing and advertising tactics of the tobacco industry."
In another ad, which the state says is designed to show that children are bombarded by tobacco imagery, cigarettes "rain" down from the sky on a Los Angeles school yard.
California previewed the ads as Liggett Group agreed on Thursday to settle tobacco litigation with almost half of the nation's attorneys general and give up potentially devastating documents.
